title: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 Explained

beats.say: It's Thursday morning, October twenty fourth, 1929, on Wall Street, the heart of America's money world. And everybody is selling.
Prices are falling so fast that the ticker can't keep up. That's a machine that prints prices on a long paper strip.
The tape's over an hour late! I don't even know how much I've lost!
Nearby, the country's top bankers meet behind closed doors. They pool their money, millions of dollars, to stop the panic.
They send one man onto the trading floor: Richard Whitney, vice president of the Stock Exchange.

tag.text: Richard Whitney, Stock Exchange vice president

beats.say: Two hundred and five for ten thousand Steel!
He's buying? Above the price? Then maybe it's all fine!
He was offering more than the current price for U.S. Steel. Traders cheered, and the panic stopped.
For a couple of days. Five days later came the worst day Wall Street had ever seen. So how did America's money party end like this? Let's find out.

show.text: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 Explained
show.sub: how borrowed money broke the world

beats.say: In the 1920s, America felt rich. The First World War was over, and factories were pumping out cars and radios.
Lots of ordinary people wanted a piece of that boom. So they bought stocks.
Here's how a stock works. A big company is split into thousands of tiny pieces called shares.
Buy one share, and you own a tiny slice of that company. If the company does well, more people want a slice, so the price goes up.
Then you sell your slice for more than you paid. Easy money! At least, that's the idea.
To keep score, people watched the Dow, short for the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It's a number that tracks thirty big companies.
When the Dow goes up, stocks are winning. When it goes down, well, you can guess.
And in the late 1920s, the Dow went up, and up, and up.
But there was a trick that made all this dangerous. It was called buying on margin.
Margin means you pay a small part of the price yourself. You borrow the rest from your stockbroker, the person who buys stocks for you.
Put down as little as ten percent, and I'll lend you the rest!
So with a hundred dollars, I get a thousand dollars of stock? Sign me up!
If the stock goes up, you're laughing. But if it goes down, the broker wants his loan back. Fast.
That demand is called a margin call. If you can't pay, the broker sells your shares, at whatever price he can get.
By 1929, everyone seemed to be buying stocks. There's even a famous story about a shoeshine boy.
It's a legend, told about Joseph Kennedy, a rich investor. It only shows up in print decades later.
Buy stocks, mister! Everybody's getting rich!
When the shoeshine boy has tips, it's time for me to get out.
Legend or not, Kennedy really did start pulling money out of the market in 1929, before the crash.
On September third, 1929, the Dow hit its peak: three hundred eighty one.

show.label: The Dow's peak, September 3, 1929
show.sub: a record it wouldn't beat for 25 years

beats.say: The first crack came from across the Atlantic Ocean, in London.
A British businessman named Clarence Hatry was caught using forged shares. His companies collapsed, and London's market dropped.
Nervous investors started to wonder if American prices had climbed too high.
But Irving Fisher, a famous economist at Yale University, told them not to worry.
Here's what he said in a speech: stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau.

show.text: Stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau.

beats.say: A plateau is high, flat land. So Fisher meant prices would just stay up there.
Nine days later, the crash began.
On Thursday, October twenty fourth, a record of nearly thirteen million shares changed hands. People call it Black Thursday.
And watching from the visitors' gallery that day was a very famous British guest.
Winston Churchill. He had just stopped being Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, the minister in charge of the country's money.
He'd also put his own money into American stocks. So he was watching his savings melt in real time.
Then the bankers' rescue kicked in, and Whitney's big bid calmed everyone down.
But over the weekend, people had time to think. And they got scared all over again.
On Monday, the Dow fell about thirteen percent. Then came Tuesday.
On October twenty ninth, Black Tuesday, everyone tried to sell at once. Almost nobody wanted to buy.
About sixteen million shares were traded in a single day. That was a record.

show.label: Shares traded on Black Tuesday
show.sub: about 16.4 million, a New York Stock Exchange record

beats.say: Remember those margin loans? Now the margin calls came pouring in.
Your stock dropped. I need more money, today!
I don't have more money! That's why I borrowed it!
So brokers sold people's shares, which pushed prices down even more. And the ticker ran hours behind, so nobody knew how bad it was.
Even stars lost big. Comedian Groucho Marx had put his savings into stocks, much of it borrowed. He said he lost about two hundred forty thousand dollars.
The next day, the show business paper Variety printed one of the most famous headlines ever.
Extra, extra! Wall Street lays an egg!
In show business, laying an egg means failing badly. And this was a very big egg.
You might have heard that ruined bankers took their own lives by the dozen. That's mostly a myth.
Historians who checked the records found no such wave. Rumors spread the story far faster than the facts.
A crash in stocks is bad. What came next was much worse: the Great Depression, the worst slump of modern times.
People who lost money stopped buying things. So factories sold less and fired workers. Then those workers stopped buying things too.
Then the banks got into trouble. A bank doesn't keep all your savings in its vault. It lends most of them out.
So if everyone wants their money back at the same time, the bank runs out. That's called a bank run.
I want my savings. All of it. Right now!
Ma'am, your money is out on loans. We have to close!
Thousands of American banks failed. Nobody insured bank savings back then, so many families lost theirs for good.
Then, in June 1930, President Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot Hawley Tariff, a big tax on goods from other countries.
Over a thousand economists begged him not to. Fun fact: one of them was Irving Fisher. Other countries hit back with their own taxes, and world trade shrank.
And the trouble crossed the ocean.
In May 1931, Austria's biggest bank, the Creditanstalt in Vienna, collapsed.
In July, the panic jumped to Germany, and big German banks failed too.
Germany had borrowed heavily from America. Now that money was being called home.
By 1932, about six million Germans were out of work. Desperate voters turned to extreme parties, including Adolf Hitler's Nazis. Hitler took power in 1933.
In September 1931, even Britain gave up the gold standard, its promise to swap pounds for gold.
Meanwhile Churchill came back to America on a lecture tour, to earn back the money he'd lost.
On December thirteenth, he crossed Fifth Avenue. Used to British traffic, he forgot to look right. A car came from the right.
Look out!
My fault entirely. I looked the wrong way!
He was badly hurt but recovered, and told police the driver wasn't to blame. Alcohol was banned in America then. So his doctor wrote him a note saying he needed it at mealtimes.
Back on Wall Street, in July 1932, the Dow finally hit bottom.
By 1933, about one in four American workers had no job.
In March 1933, a new president took over: Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Two days in, he closed every bank in the country. He called it a bank holiday. Some holiday.
Then he went on the radio, in a talk called a fireside chat, to calm everyone down.
He said: I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress.

show.text: I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress.
show.who: Franklin D. Roosevelt, first fireside chat, March 12, 1933

beats.say: That year, Congress also created the FDIC, which insures bank savings. If an insured bank fails, your money is protected.
In 1934 came the SEC, a new watchdog for the stock market. Its first boss? Joseph Kennedy, the man from the shoeshine legend.
Critics said a market insider was the wrong man. Roosevelt reportedly joked: set a thief to catch a thief.
And Richard Whitney, the hero of Black Thursday? He became president of the Stock Exchange. Then he got caught stealing other people's money.
In 1938, he went to Sing Sing prison.
And the Dow? It didn't climb back to its 1929 peak until November 1954.

show.label: Time for the Dow to get back to its 1929 peak

beats.say: So, what's the lesson? Borrowed money makes the party bigger, and the crash much worse.
And when a smart person says prices will stay high forever, maybe check twice.
Next up: the Medici, the bankers who bought the Pope. Watch it next, and subscribe.

description:
In 1929, Americans bought stocks with borrowed money, and on Black Tuesday it all came crashing down, with about 16 million shares dumped in a single day. We explain stocks, margin and the Dow in plain words, then follow Churchill, Groucho Marx, Joseph Kennedy and the Stock Exchange hero who ended up in Sing Sing prison, as the crash turned into the Great Depression.
